extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers, students of literature, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for judging poets, poetic genres (epic, tragedy, lyric), and qualities that make poetry enduring or effective, offered in the form of a literary essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for the unities, rhythm, and rhyme
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet 'must respect the unities, and be loyal to rhythm and rhyme,' or he cannot induce the critics even to blast him with their thunders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes that while some poets revolt against these canons (a 'wild colt' of a bardling), critics' disapproval usually kills or tames such revolt; examples given include MacDonald Clarke and Walt Whitman (original but unlikely to gain orthodox critical honors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin in close observation and solitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry often springs from lives of solitude and watchful observation — e.g., 'the earliest poets were... the shepherds' whose loneliness and alert senses predispose them to poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The shepherd's life sharpens perception and leads to loftier meditations that melt into poetry; the essay uses pastoral origins (Book of Job, shepherd-boy David) to argue for a source of authentic poetic feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic: heroic, majestic presentation of human life
rubrics_metrics.description: The Epic 'embodied and presented human life under its more heroic and majestic aspects' and functioned, historically, like the modern novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay observes that epics tend to be enjoyed more as objects of study ('delight of association') than direct simple pleasure for unclassical youth, implying that epic's stature is formal and associative rather than immediately accessible entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy: struggle of Man with Misfortune; Virtue enduring Adversity
rubrics_metrics.description: The argument of Tragedy is 'the struggle of Man with Misfortune, — the spectacle of Virtue enduring the buffets of Adversity, and of Crime overtaken by the shafts of Retribution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greek Tragedy is praised for presenting the undaunted human soul defying Fate (Prometheus example); tragedy should teach stoical endurance, intellectual force, and moral law — Good as the true end of Power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and philosophical depth (stoical endurance, moral law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great tragic poetry (e.g., Prometheus) conveys stoical endurance and asserts that all forces are subject to moral law; the lesson is without a modern parallel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such works are not irreverent to religion but dramatize eternal truths (Good as measure of Power); moral depth elevates tragedy beyond spectacle into instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and originality versus second-hand 'lamp' literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Works that 'smell of the lamp' or are second-hand lack true poetic quality; Roman literature is criticized as not truly poetic because much of it is derivative of Greece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet/nation's literature should not be merely imitative; originality and organic development (not dependence on predecessors) are marks of genuine poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct enjoyment versus learned association
rubrics_metrics.description: Some great works (epics) are read mainly by those 'impelled to study them as a task' rather than for direct and simple enjoyment; true poetic greatness includes the capacity for direct pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts epics with more popularly read works (Arabian Nights, Dickens) to show that accessibility and immediate enjoyment are important measures of a poem's impact on general readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and directness of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry 'should embody the soul's higher and purer emotions in the simplest and directest terms which the language affords' — intensity of expression and profusion of superlatives are out of place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented via Wordsworth's aesthetic: restraint, plainness, and purity of feeling are virtues; excessive vehemence or ornamental excess weakens poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between verse-making skill and true poetic genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Some writers (e.g., Pope) are 'the king of verse-makers' yet may not be poets in the highest sense; much of their verse would read like prose if rewritten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical mastery, cleverness, and polished workmanship do not equal the deeper qualities of poetry — sincerity, imaginative depth, and lasting human significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry that speaks from the heart—truth and nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry must 'speak once more to the soul in accents of Truth and Nature' — Burns is credited with brushing aside artificial conceits and restoring honest, manly voice to poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessible, authentic voice that addresses common experience and moral truth makes poetry enduring and widely appreciated (appeals across drawing-room and log-cabin alike).

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive power and vivid imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive faculty ('Description is my forte' — Byron) and vivid scenes that embody impressions (e.g., Manfred's Coliseum passage) are a major poetic strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability to embody impressions and emotions through striking description can make passages widely remembered and influential; travel/landscape description can be especially evocative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's capacity to move and address universal human feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain poets (e.g., David's Psalms) 'sweep the chords of the human heart' and provide fuller, fitter expressions of aspirations and needs across ages and races.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The power to touch fundamental human emotions — penitence, aspiration, awe — is a criterion for poetic greatness; poems that teach how to implore forgiveness and help are ennobling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence on the age and moral consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's influence (Byron's effect on the century) and the moral consequences of that influence (not always good) factor into his place in literary history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widespread readership and the social/moral impact of a poet's ideas are part of their evaluation — influence may be praised or criticized depending on its effect on faith, morals, and public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance/tenacity in artistic practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenacity can secure eventual critical acceptance (Wordsworth's perseverance led to triumph despite early jeers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistence in a consistent poetic approach, even under critical hostility, can vindicate a poet's principles and style over time; critics may change position once the practice is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: National-poetic originality and translatability
rubrics_metrics.description: To create a 'National Poetry' one must produce work other nations eagerly translate and treasure; many competent verse-makers fail to achieve this international, lasting stature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond technical facility, a poet must capture qualities of universal appeal and depth that invite translation and long-term cross-cultural appreciation to be considered foundational for a nation's literature.
